steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on using a physics-enhanced multi-fidelity neural network to infer a material's stress-strain behaviour from the optical profile of an indentation imprint. Cover the background on indentation and on AI for science, our approach and network design, and a list of contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Searching for materials; indentation as a high-throughput probe; optical measurement
- AI for science: scarce data and inverse problems
- Our approach: residual pattern to stress-strain curve, checking non-uniqueness
- NN architecture: 2D to 3D to experiments, tuning physical parameters
- Contributions

  - inverse problems: input-output relation may be ill-conditioned (cite)
  - different inputs -> similar/same outputs -> inaccurate NN inference back to inputs = non-unique problem

  - optimize inverse mapping: residual indentation pattern -> stress-strain curve, via MFNN
  - first NN for forward problem + optimization to search for non-uniqueness; helps choose features
  - finding: residual pattern informative enough, not load-displacement curve

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
For the past century, people have been looking for natural or artificial materials with the most suitable mechanical properties. To speed up this search, a lot of research has gone into building platforms for high-throughput (HT) synthesis and characterization of materials. Because it is simple to do experimentally and can be applied widely, indentation has been seen as a paradigm for HT probing of the mechanical properties of materials. Indentation needs very little specimen preparation and mounting, gives hundreds of data from one specimen, and can probe materials from the nano to the macro scale by changing the load. When a sharp indenter is pushed into the material surface under a constant load, the surface gets crashed and forms a crown-like pattern, and this pattern has a lot of information that reveals the elasto-plastic properties of the material. But the inverse mapping from the crashed pattern to formal material parameters is quite complex, so many earlier researchers just used the pattern information as a rough criterion. On the other hand, measuring the optical profile directly is more convenient than traditional characterization methods like tensile testing. Optical measurement has been used in many areas, for example biological systems, particle tracking and vibrations.

The fast development of artificial intelligence has created a big opportunity of AI for science. One big limitation is that in many scientific areas there is not much data, especially high-fidelity experimental data. To deal with this, many new machine learning frameworks that include physical constraints have been proposed, e.g. physics-informed neural networks (PINN). Some pre-training and transfer learning frameworks have also been proposed so that less real experimental data is needed. A rough model is trained on lots of simulation data and then fine-tuned with some experimental data, and this way less high-fidelity data is needed. Another big issue in scientific AI is that many problems in science are inverse problems, i.e. the input-output relation can be ill-conditioned. Sometimes different input parameters give similar or even the same output results, which makes the NN prediction inaccurate when we try to infer from the results back to the inputs. This is called the non-unique problem.

Here, we try to optimize the inverse mapping from the residual pattern made by indentation to the formal stress-strain curve of the material, using MFNN. To make sure the problem is not ill-conditioned and the model can predict well, we first use a NN to explore the forward problem and then combine it with an optimization method to search for possible non-uniqueness. This helps to decide which features are suitable to choose. What we found scientifically is that the residual pattern, and not the load-displacement curve, is already informative enough to predict the stress-strain relation. This turns out to agree with earlier mechanical theories of strain fields.

- NN architecture
  - initial NN on lots of 2D FEM (finite element methods) simulation data -> transferred to 3D with some 3D FEM data
  - fine-tuned with real experimental data + physical constraints
  - tune friction coefficient \mu and Poisson’s ratio \nu in simulation set -> ensemble of three parallel NNs -> final model
  - tuning step critical for accuracy: closer sim-to-real gap
  - satisfying accuracy on real stress-strain of testing materials
  - pre-assumed material model strongly influences result -> method without pre-assumed model, relatively good accuracy

- Contributions
  - first NN framework inverting optical profile of indentation imprint to real elasto-plastic properties; models with/without pre-defined mechanical laws
  - MFNN combining 2D + 3D FEM + real experiments; physical intuitions reduce data needs, stabilize model; needs experimental data of only 3 types of materials; experimental results for other 20; average 3.4% relative error over 20 testing materials
  - forward NN + BFGS optimization (cite) to explore non-uniqueness and find required features; NN forward models increasingly used in computational imaging; speeding up / differentiating FEM effective application
  - release dataset + code; MFNN as benchmark

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
For the past century, people have been looking for natural or artificial materials with the most suitable mechanical properties. To speed up this search, a lot of research has gone into building platforms for high-throughput (HT) synthesis and characterization of materials. Because it is simple to do experimentally and can be applied widely, indentation has been seen as a paradigm for HT probing of the mechanical properties of materials. Indentation needs very little specimen preparation and mounting, gives hundreds of data from one specimen, and can probe materials from the nano to the macro scale by changing the load. When a sharp indenter is pushed into the material surface under a constant load, the surface gets crashed and forms a crown-like pattern, and this pattern has a lot of information that reveals the elasto-plastic properties of the material. But the inverse mapping from the crashed pattern to formal material parameters is quite complex, so many earlier researchers just used the pattern information as a rough criterion. On the other hand, measuring the optical profile directly is more convenient than traditional characterization methods like tensile testing. Optical measurement has been used in many areas, for example biological systems, particle tracking and vibrations.

The fast development of artificial intelligence has created a big opportunity of AI for science. One big limitation is that in many scientific areas there is not much data, especially high-fidelity experimental data. To deal with this, many new machine learning frameworks that include physical constraints have been proposed, e.g. physics-informed neural networks (PINN). Some pre-training and transfer learning frameworks have also been proposed so that less real experimental data is needed. A rough model is trained on lots of simulation data and then fine-tuned with some experimental data, and this way less high-fidelity data is needed. Another big issue in scientific AI is that many problems in science are inverse problems, i.e. the input-output relation can be ill-conditioned. Sometimes different input parameters give similar or even the same output results, which makes the NN prediction inaccurate when we try to infer from the results back to the inputs. This is called the non-unique problem.

Here, we try to optimize the inverse mapping from the residual pattern made by indentation to the formal stress-strain curve of the material, using MFNN. To make sure the problem is not ill-conditioned and the model can predict well, we first use a NN to explore the forward problem and then combine it with an optimization method to search for possible non-uniqueness. This helps to decide which features are suitable to choose. What we found scientifically is that the residual pattern, and not the load-displacement curve, is already informative enough to predict the stress-strain relation. This turns out to agree with earlier mechanical theories of strain fields.

For the NN architecture, we first build an initial NN model from a large amount of 2D simulation data from finite element methods (FEM), and then transfer it into the 3D model using some 3D FEM simulation data. The transferred model is then fine-tuned further by adding some real experimental data and the corresponding physical constraints. To make the transfer learning more efficient and stable, we tune two physical parameters in the simulation set (friction coefficient \mu and Poisson’s ratio \nu), which gives an ensemble of three parallel NNs. The final model is built from these NNs. It turns out that tuning the physical parameters is a very critical step for the prediction accuracy. The reason is that the sim-to-real gap gets smaller after tuning the friction coefficient \mu and Poisson’s ratio \nu. The final result has satisfying accuracy when predicting the real stress-strain relation of the testing materials. We also notice that the material model we assume at the start to describe material behaviors has a big influence on the final prediction. So we also propose a method that does not pre-assume a material model, and it gets relatively good accuracy. In summary, the main contributions of the paper are:

- To the best of our knowledge, this is the first attempt to use a NN framework to invert the optical profile of the indentation imprint into the real elasto-plastic properties of the material. We train and discuss models both with and without pre-defined mechanical laws.

- We design the MFNN framework to combine multi-fidelity data from 2D and 3D FEM simulation and from real experiments. We add physical intuitions into the MFNN model to reduce how much data is needed and to make the model stable. The model only needs real experimental data from 3 types of materials. We also contribute experimental results for 20 other types of materials. Our model gets an average 3.4% relative error over the 20 real testing materials.

- We use a forward NN and BFGS optimization to look into the non-unique issue in the inverse problem and to find the features that are needed for training. NN-based approaches that approximate forward models are a powerful tool and have been used more in computational imaging recently. Our work adds that using this kind of approach to speed up and differentiate FEM is an effective application.

- We release the dataset and code for indentation and the corresponding residual imprint features. Our MFNN framework can be used as a benchmark for this problem.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Over the past century, humans have been searching for natural or artificial materials with the most suitable mechanical properties. To accelerate this search, persistent research has focused on developing platforms for high-throughput (HT) synthesis and characterization of materials [1,2]. Thanks to its intrinsic experimental simplicity and broad applicability, indentation has been regarded as a paradigm for HT probing of the mechanical properties of materials [3,4]. Indentation requires minimal specimen preparation and mounting, yields hundreds of data from a single specimen, and can probe materials from nano to macro scales via varied loads [5,6]. When a sharp indenter is pushed into the material surface under a constant load, the surface is crashed to form a crown-like pattern containing plentiful information that reveals the elasto-plastic properties of the material. However, since the inverse mapping from the crashed pattern to formal material parameters is quite complex, many former researchers treated the pattern information only as a rough criterion [7]. On the other hand, compared to traditional characterization methods like tensile testing, direct measurement of the optical profile is more convenient. Optical measurement has been widely applied in many areas, such as biological systems [8,9], particle tracking [10] and vibrations [11,12].

The rapid development of artificial intelligence has created a great opportunity for AI for science [13,14,15]. One big limitation is that data in many scientific areas are not plentiful, especially high-fidelity experimental data. To overcome this problem, many new machine learning frameworks incorporating physical constraints have been proposed, e.g., physics-informed neural networks (PINN) [11,16]. To reduce the need for real experimental data, some pre-training and transfer learning frameworks have been proposed: a rough model is trained with plenty of simulation data and then fine-tuned with some experimental data, which lowers the requirement for high-fidelity data. Another big issue in scientific AI is that many scientific problems are inverse problems, i.e., the input-output relation may be ill-conditioned [17,18,19,20]. Sometimes different input parameters correspond to similar or even identical output results, making the NN prediction inaccurate when inferring the results back to the inputs. This is referred to as the non-unique problem.

Herein, we attempt to optimize the inverse mapping from the residual pattern formed by indentation to the formal stress-strain curve of materials through MFNN. To ensure our problem is not ill-conditioned so that the model can predict well, we first apply a NN to explore the forward problem and then combine it with an optimization method to search for possible non-uniqueness. This method helps determine which features are suitable to choose. Our scientific discovery is that, instead of the load-displacement curve, the residual pattern is already informative enough to predict the stress-strain relation. This conclusion turns out to be consistent with former mechanical theories of strain fields.

As for the NN architecture, the whole process starts by building an initial NN model based on a large amount of 2D simulation data from finite element methods (FEM), which is then transferred into the 3D model using some 3D FEM simulation data. The transferred model is further fine-tuned by incorporating some real experimental data and the corresponding physical constraints. To make the transfer learning process more efficient and stable, two physical parameters (friction coefficient \mu and Poisson’s ratio \nu) are tuned in the simulation set, resulting in an ensemble of three parallel NNs from which the final model is constructed. This step of tuning physical parameters turns out to be quite critical to the prediction accuracy, owing to the closer sim-to-real gap after tuning the friction coefficient \mu and Poisson’s ratio \nu. The final result achieves satisfying accuracy when predicting the real stress-strain relation of the testing materials. We further notice that the material model pre-assumed to describe material behaviors strongly influences the final prediction. Hence, a method without a pre-assumed material model is proposed and achieves relatively good accuracy. In summary, the main contributions of the paper include:

- To the best of our knowledge, the first attempt to apply a NN framework to inverting the optical profile of the indentation imprint into the real elasto-plastic properties of materials. Models with and without pre-defined mechanical laws are respectively trained and discussed.

- Designing the MFNN framework to combine multi-fidelity data from 2D and 3D FEM simulation and real experiments, and incorporating physical intuitions into the MFNN model to decrease the data requirements and stabilize the model. The constructed model only needs real experimental data of 3 types of materials. We also contribute experimental results for 20 other types of materials. Our model achieves an average 3.4% relative error across the 20 real testing materials.

- Applying a forward NN and BFGS [21] optimization to explore the non-unique issue in the inverse problem and identify the features required for training. NN-based approaches that approximate forward models are a powerful tool that has recently seen more use in computational imaging. Our work shows that using such an approach to speed up and differentiate FEM is an effective application.

- Release of the dataset and code for indentation and the corresponding residual imprint features. Our MFNN framework can serve as a benchmark for this problem.
